reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: The 45-home-run projection is the easiest part to believe. At 93.1 mph average exit velocity and a 51.6% hard-hit rate, Caminero hits the ball as hard as almost anyone in the league, and the .375 xwOBA says the contact quality isn't just loud — it's translating. His 12.6% walk rate keeps the OBP honest even when pitchers try to work around him, which they will more often as he ages into the middle of a lineup. The one thing holding this profile below truly elite territory is the defense: an OAA percentile sitting at 1 means he's a liability at third, and if Tampa eventually moves him off the position, the offensive profile has to carry the whole profile without any positional credit helping it.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power combination is genuinely freakish: a 21.9% barrel rate and 95.1 mph average exit velocity both sit at the top of the Statcast leaderboard, and a 16.6% walk rate keeps him on base at a clip that makes .385 OBP feel conservative rather than ambitious. The problem is the 29.3% strikeout rate, and a 31.1% whiff rate tells you the swing-and-miss isn't just sequencing noise. The whole profile hinges on whether Wood can hold that chase rate, currently 22.3%, as pitchers map out his weaknesses over a full second season, because if that number climbs, the strikeouts follow and the .423 xwOBA stops translating. If discipline holds, the projection's 40 home runs in 740 plate appearances is the floor of a conversation, not the ceiling.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .361 xwOBA tells you what the strikeouts are obscuring. Crow-Armstrong chases at a 34.4% clip and whiffs at 28.2%, numbers that push his K% to 26.2%, but his 11.8% walk rate and 47.8% hard-hit rate mean the contact he makes is doing real damage, and the Statcast picture is materially better than the surface line suggests. At 29.5 ft/s sprint speed he sits at the 96th percentile, which turns singles into threats and gives the 38 projected stolen bases a legitimate foundation. If the chase rate tightens even modestly, the projection of .273/.362/.500 with 32 home runs starts to look conservative; if it doesn't, you're still looking at a plus-run, plus-power outfielder whose floor is a second-division regular on name alone but whose actual profile is considerably more interesting than that.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast batting profile sits at .410 xwOBA and .571 xSLG, both in the 98th percentile, while the pitching side shows a 2.71 xERA and a 30.4% whiff rate — and those numbers belong to the same person. The one genuine tension in his hitting profile is that 29.6% whiff rate against a 14.2% walk rate: he misses a lot, but he draws a walk in more than one of every seven plate appearances, which keeps the on-base floor from collapsing even when pitchers attack him. On the mound, the barrel rate against him is 3.8%, which tells you hitters aren't squaring him up even when they make contact. If it works across a full Dodger season, you're looking at a .928 OPS hitter and a frontline starter sharing a roster spot; if the elbow history dictates a reduced pitching role, what remains at the plate is still one of the most complete offensive profiles in baseball.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: A 2.76 xERA with a 5.6% walk rate is the profile of a legitimate frontline starter, not a guy running hot on sequencing luck. Skenes gets hitters out at a 29.7% strikeout clip while barely issuing free passes, and a 33.9% chase rate explains how: batters are expanding, chasing out of the zone rather than simply missing pitches over the plate. The projection, 3.25 ERA over 183.8 innings with 221 strikeouts, is a slight step back from what the Statcast profile says he's actually been, which means if the chase rate holds and the control stays sharp, that ERA could settle closer to the expected number than the projected one.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The bat-to-ball profile is the one thing standing between Walker and a clear top-of-the-order future. His 93.7 mph average exit velocity sits at the 97th percentile, the barrel rate is 14.0%, and the underlying contact grades (.282 xBA, .502 xSLG) suggest the raw power translates even when the actual line doesn't look like it. The problem is a 35.4% chase rate and a 30.6% whiff rate that keep the strikeouts near 24.7%, which means a significant chunk of that contact quality gets wasted on swings he shouldn't offer. If the zone management tightens even modestly, the projection's .827 OPS and 31 home runs across 665 plate appearances is probably a floor; if it doesn't, you're still getting a dangerous middle-of-the-order bat, just one who costs you more outs than he should at 23.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .306, 99th percentile, and the contact quality underneath it is what makes the .282 projection feel conservative rather than hopeful. At 92.9 mph average exit velocity and 52.2% hard-hit rate, he's doing elite contact damage, and the 30.3 ft/s sprint speed converts a portion of that damage that would retire anyone else. The one friction point is a 33.0% chase rate, which suppresses his walk opportunities and is the reason the OBP projection stays at .351 despite the raw contact ability; if that rate tightens even modestly, the offensive profile takes a significant step up. He's already a true shortstop, a 42-steal threat in projection, and a .819 OPS hitter — the question isn't whether he's good, it's how long before the chase discipline catches up to everything else he already is.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: mid-rotation starter or better with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 77.7 AA IP.
reports.published_report: A 1.3 ERA and a 0.60 WHIP at Double-A, across 77.7 innings, is the kind of line that makes you look for the catch. Ten walks in 276 batters faced — that's the whole argument. The translation puts his K/9 at 10.0 and his BB/9 at 2.0, where the MLB average sits at 3.2, which means the control isn't a mirage of a favorable environment but something that carries into an MLB context with real separation, and a K-BB% translating to 21.9% beside a 13.5% MLB norm is the same story told twice. If Anderson's stuff plays at the next level the way the command profile suggests it will, he's a mid-rotation starter at the floor; if the stuff doesn't hold, 115 strikeouts built on elite control still leaves a pitcher with a job.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is extreme and it's right there in the contact numbers: an 18.4% walk rate sitting alongside a 36.8% whiff rate, both near the outer edges of what the majors see. Kurtz generates 93.6 mph average exit velocity with an 18.1% barrel rate, which is why the .379 xwOBA reads as legitimate despite a .250 xBA — he destroys what he makes contact with, but he swings through a lot of pitches first. The whole profile hinges on whether pitchers can force him into more two-strike counts and shrink that walk rate, because a 31.6% strikeout rate is already a significant tax on the production. If the contact rates hold where they are, the projection's .898 OPS with 31 home runs is a fair accounting of what he produces; if pitchers learn to attack him within the zone and his 22.8% chase rate creeps up, the strikeouts compound and the walks evaporate, and you're left with raw power trapped inside a very lossy profile.

His 30.5% strikeout rate leans on that chase, not on whiff volume inside, the 27.8% Whiff% is functional, not elite, so the profile is more get-ahead-and-make-them-chase than pure swing-and-miss. reports.name: Juan Soto
reports.published_report: A .422 xwOBA tells you what he is before you even get to the walk rate. Soto chases 19.8% of pitches out of the zone, strikes out just 13.4% of the time, and draws a walk on 17.5% of plate appearances, a combination that doesn't leave pitchers much room to work, which is why the projection lands at a .412 OBP across 605 plate appearances. The contact quality backs the discipline: a .589 xSLG and 14.3% barrel rate say the 34-home-run projection is earned, not optimistic. reports.name: Zach Neto
reports.published_report: The barrel rate tells you what Neto is: 12.9% puts him in genuine power territory for a shortstop, and the projection leans into it with 29 home runs across 703 projected plate appearances. The problem is everything around contact. A 31.6% strikeout rate and a 36.3% chase rate suppress his xBA to .204, which is why the xwOBA sits at .309 despite the barrel quality, and why the counting line looks stranger than it should, 29 homers against a .237 average. The 10.2% walk rate keeps him from being a total liability at the top of an inning, and the speed is real enough to support 23 steals, so the profile works as a fantasy asset if you squint past the batting average crater. This is a shortstop who hits for power the way a corner bat does, keeps the lineup moving, and costs you something every time he swings at a pitch off the plate, which he does constantly.

reports.name: Tyler Bremner
reports.peak_summary: Projection: back end starter with medium risk. The current pitching shape is mixed over 38.3 A+ IP.
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud; the translation is the problem. At A+ in 2026, Bremner has punched out 51 batters across 38.3 innings, a 12.0 K/9 that ranks in the 84th percentile among pitchers with 20-plus innings, and his 21% K-BB% sits at the 89th percentile in the same pool. Translate that to an MLB-equivalent context and the strikeout rate compresses to 8.7 K/9, barely above what pitchers face leaguewide, while the walk rate stays elevated and the K-BB% lands at 13.3% where the MLB average is 13.5%. The whole profile hinges on whether the swing-and-miss translates up the ladder or whether what looks like a weapon at A+ is simply level-driven, and with only 38 innings of evidence the confidence here is genuinely low. If the strikeout rate holds shape as he climbs, there's a back-end starter; if it flattens to what the translation already suggests, you're looking at a depth arm.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with medium risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 196 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The contact is the calling card, and the swing-and-miss is almost nonexistent. Across AAA & A+ & A this season, Jenkins is striking out at just a 14% clip over 213 plate appearances, which translates to an 18.6% MLB-equivalent rate, well short of what most hitters post in the majors, and he's pairing that with 27 walks against only 30 strikeouts. The power, though, is where the conversation gets honest: a .19 ISO in the minors flattens to a .147 MLB-equivalent, nearly indistinguishable from the MLB mean of .150, which means if the game power doesn't develop beyond what's here, he becomes a high-contact, on-base-oriented center fielder who lives on the fringes of everyday status rather than holding it comfortably. A low-end everyday regular if the bat-to-ball skills carry and the power ticks forward; a useful bench piece if the contact stays but the power stalls exactly where it is.

reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: That 38.7% chase rate is the engine, 99th percentile, the kind of number that makes hitters expand the zone before they've decided to swing. Pair it with a 4.5% walk rate and a 32.4% whiff rate and you have a pitcher who manufactures swing-and-miss without losing the zone, which is the rarest combination a starting pitcher can carry. The contact he does allow comes in hard, 43.8% hard-hit rate, so the profile hinges entirely on hitters continuing to chase pitches they can't do damage on when they find them. If that chase rate erodes and hitters lay off long enough to wait for something they can drive, the hard contact becomes a real problem, but right now the sequencing keeps it dormant, and a 2.80 ERA projection over 205.3 innings reflects exactly that fragile-looking-but-functional balance.

reports.name: MacKenzie Gore

reports.name: Bryce Elder
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 3.86 while the ERA projection runs a half-run hotter, and that gap is the whole argument about Elder. His calling card is barrel suppression, holding hitters to a 6.0% barrel rate, but he gets there with a 92.6 mph fastball that generates a 22.5% whiff rate — soft contact allowed, not swing-and-miss earned. The strikeout rate at 19.7% is the vulnerability; if opposing lineups stop chasing and start working counts, that contact-management profile thins out fast. What he probably is: a back-of-rotation starter who logs serious innings, keeps the walks manageable at 7.2%, and gives Atlanta a steady if unexciting rotation piece rather than anything they can rely on in October.

reports.name: Trea Turner
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile says a lot about why Turner's last couple of years have been disappointing: a .295 xwOBA sitting in the 20th percentile, a 35.0% chase rate also in the 20th percentile, and a 6.3% walk rate near the bottom of the league. What he still owns is the 98th-percentile sprint speed at 29.8 ft/s, and the projection leans on it hard, carrying 27 stolen bases and 102 runs in 698 plate appearances even as the bat reads as a below-average offensive profile. The whole thing hinges on whether the contact and discipline numbers stabilize enough to let the speed stay productive, because a .302 OBP attached to a .251 average leaves almost no margin for a cold stretch at the plate.

reports.name: Kahlil Watson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 264 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The power and the plate discipline both grade, and that's the tension: it's not often you see a 23-year-old center field prospect draw 37 walks while also posting a .226 ISO at AAA, but the strikeouts are the ceiling limiter. At 29% at AAA, the K% translates to 27.2% in MLB context, and a league that averages 22.0% has a way of exposing hitters who can't close that kind of gap. The walk rate and the raw power both survive the translation, landing at 11.0% BB% and a .168 ISO, which is a real offensive profile — just one that depends entirely on whether the bat-to-ball improves enough for pitchers to stop hunting him. If it does, he's a bottom-of-the-order everyday center fielder; if it doesn't, the power and the walks make him a useful bench bat, not a regular.

reports.name: Andre Pallante
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 3.72 while the projection calls for a 4.11 ERA, and that gap is the whole argument. Pallante gets contact on the ground and keeps it soft, a 6.1% barrel rate and 34.5% hard-hit rate that both land in the upper quarter of the league, doing it almost entirely without swing-and-miss, because a 16.9% strikeout rate and 20.3% whiff rate are both near the bottom of the rotation tier. The walk rate at 7.0% is quietly doing real work here, keeping counts clean enough that he can survive without chasing swings. If the contact management holds, he's a durable back-of-the-rotation starter who earns a full workload; if hitters start squaring him up more consistently, there's not enough strikeout upside to compensate.

reports.name: Michael McGreevy
reports.published_report:
The 3.49 ERA projection and the 5.44 xERA are not really arguing with each other. One of them is right, and the Statcast profile says which one.

His 16.3 K% sits at the 10th percentile, his 18.7 Whiff% is at the 6th, and a 91.7 mph fastball at the 7th — that's a pitcher who can't miss bats and can't blow them by anybody. The one thing actually working is a 5.9 BB% at the 87th percentile, which keeps counts manageable and explains how he strings together quality starts without swing-and-miss. Everything hinges on that command holding and the defense behind him staying clean, because a .355 xwOBA against him means hitters are making real contact when they do connect, and if either slips the ERA catches up to the xERA fast, leaving a back-end arm who needs every break to go right.

reports.name: Rafael Devers
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the power metrics are telling two different stories, and understanding Devers means knowing which one to believe. His 92.3 mph average exit velocity and 50.7% hard-hit rate are genuinely elite, the ball comes off the bat loud and often, but a 29.9% whiff rate and .229 xBA say he's giving a lot of that back through swing-and-miss. The gap between those two pictures collapses into a .320 xwOBA that sits right at the middle of the league, which is the honest summary: a corner bat who generates 31 projected home runs but costs you something in the average column. The whole profile hinges on whether pitchers keep attacking him the way they do, because if the strikeout rate climbs further the .787 OPS fades toward roster-filler territory fast, but if the contact just holds where it is, you've got a productive middle-of-the-order thumper at a position that doesn't demand more.

reports.name: Kyle Schwarber
reports.published_report: Forty-eight projected home runs and a .357 OBP at 33 is a number most teams would take from a player half his age, but the Statcast profile explains exactly how a 34.8% strikeout rate and a .238 xBA coexist with a .368 xWOBA. He barrels the ball at an 18.6% clip, an average exit velocity of 93.3 mph, and a 52.3% hard-hit rate, which means when he makes contact it is genuinely punishing — the walk rate of 14.0% does the rest of the damage, keeping him on base even when the strikeouts pile up. The profile is simple: the power and patience carry him, and if either erodes with age, the average offers no floor to stand on. A .526 projected SLG with that contact profile is what it looks like when one skill is elite enough to run the whole operation.

reports.published_report: The xwOBA (.247) and xERA (2.50) both sit at the 98th percentile, which means the underlying quality here is as good as it gets in a bullpen — and the reason it holds up is the chase rate. Getting hitters to expand at a 35.0% clip does the work that raw stuff alone can't, keeping hard contact ordinary even when it lands. Thirty saves and a 2.35 ERA across 73.2 innings is closer-caliber production, and the Statcast profile gives you reason to trust the shape of it rather than just the number. The one dependency: if that 6.3% walk rate drifts north, the whole profile tightens, because the margin for error in a profile built on chase rather than pure velocity is smaller than it looks.

reports.name: Bryce Harper
reports.published_report: The .381 xwOBA tells you most of what you need to know: elite contact quality, elite walk rate at 14.4%, and a profile that keeps producing even when the raw exit velocity sits at 90.2 mph. Harper is doing it with pitch selection and angle, not pure brute force, which is worth noting at 33. The 31.3% whiff rate and 34.5% chase rate are genuine liabilities that keep him from being a truly clean hitter, and if pitchers find a way to exploit that further, the strikeout rate climbs off its current median perch and the .258 projection average gets squeaky. If the zone control holds, you get a full-season .488 SLG, 32 home runs, and one of the more durable offensive profiles in the Philadelphia lineup.

reports.name: Landen Roupp
reports.published_report: The contact suppression numbers are striking for a guy whose fastball sits at 93.0 mph with 2157 rpm spin. A 30.1% hard-hit rate and 4.1% barrel rate tell you hitters aren't squaring him up, and that combination doesn't usually belong to a pitcher with below-average raw stuff. The walk rate is the thing to watch: 9.8% BB% undercuts what the xERA of 3.36 suggests he can be, because that control problem is the difference between a mid-rotation workhorse and a pitcher who beats himself in the third time through. If he tightens the zone and the contact-suppression holds, the projection's 3.9 ERA across 166.1 innings looks conservative; if it doesn't, you're looking at a back-end starter who occasionally flashes better.

reports.name: Nasim Nuñez
reports.published_report: Fifty stolen bases in 488 projected plate appearances is the entire argument, and the contact and power profile underneath it is genuinely grim. An xSLG of .275 sits at the 1st percentile, average exit velocity of 84.7 mph at the 3rd, and a 0.5% barrel rate that rounds to nothing — the bat generates almost no damage when it connects. What saves the profile is a 26.3% chase rate paired with a 10.2% walk rate, meaning he reaches base enough and runs aggressively enough to manufacture value that his raw offensive numbers wouldn't suggest. If the speed ages or the stolen-base rate regresses, what remains is a .622 OPS bat with no power, and that profile has no everyday home; what works is a top-of-the-order disruptor who turns a weak-contact skill set into runs through volume and legs.

reports.name: Seiya Suzuki
reports.published_report: The chase rate tells most of the story: 22.4% puts him in the 91st percentile, and an 11.7% walk rate does the rest of the work explaining why a guy with middling exit velocity keeps posting useful offensive numbers. His average exit velocity of 89.1 mph and 40.8% hard-hit rate are both right around league average, so the power, projected at 26 home runs across 608 plate appearances, comes from a 9.9% barrel rate squeezing every bit out of what contact he does make. The whole profile hinges on that discipline holding; if pitchers ever find a way to attack him inside the zone and force swings he can't handle, the strikeout rate at 25.5% is already the weak link. A .812 OPS contributor who earns his way on base more than he crushes it, a solid and slightly underrated middle-of-the-order piece with a real floor.

reports.name: Gage Jump
reports.published_report: The fastball sits at 96.3 mph with 2355 rpm spin, and a 31.7% chase rate shows hitters are respecting the shape of his stuff. The problem is contact quality: a 43.1% hard-hit rate and 90.3 mph average exit velo say that when hitters do connect, they connect flush, and a 23.6% whiff rate is too thin to paper over that. The xERA of 4.22 and a projected 1.4 WHIP tell the same story, a guy with a plus fastball who hasn't figured out how to miss enough bats to keep the barrel rate from mattering. If the whiff rate climbs as the arsenal develops, you've got a back-end starter; if it doesn't, 115.9 projected innings of below-average contact management is a tough way to hold rotation space at 22.

reports.published_report: Eleven percent barrels, 12.3% walks, and a .178 xBA: that's the whole tension. Raleigh makes enough contact to barrel the ball at a useful rate, walks at a clip that most catchers can't match, but misses so often, 31.7% strikeouts against a chase rate of 37.1%, that the actual batting average collapses and the projection lands at .186/.290/.366. The barrel rate and a .352 xSLG say the power translates when he connects, but the contact hole is wide enough that 22 projected home runs across 520 plate appearances still produces an OPS of .656, which is replacement-level offense dressed up in counting stats. If the chase rate ever comes down even a tick, the walk rate suggests he has the eye to convert that into something useful; if it doesn't, he's a below-average bat the Mariners tolerate because catchers who walk at 12.3% don't grow on trees.

reports.name: Freddy Peralta
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile and the projection are telling two different stories, and that gap is the whole read. His xERA sits at 3.83 and his xwOBA at .303, both comfortably better than a league-average starter, yet ValuCast projects a 4.63 ERA over 172.5 innings — the difference lives almost entirely in his walk rate. A 9.3% BB% is the anchor dragging him; the whiff rate at 26.6% is fine, but hitters don't need to chase him at 28.8% because he'll eventually come to them. What saves contact when it does happen is genuine: 2423 rpm on the fastball and a 5.4% barrel rate suggest the stuff plays up in quality even if the command doesn't hold the zone, and 87.8 mph average exit velocity reflects that. If the walk rate tightens even modestly, the underlying contact profile points toward a mid-rotation arm; if it stays where it is, that 4.63 ERA is about right for what he delivers.

reports.name: Luis Perales
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 73.7 AAA IP.
reports.published_report:
The ERA looks good. The walk rate says don't trust it.

At AAA in 2026, Perales carries a 3.7 ERA and 1.3 WHIP across 73.7 innings, and those surface numbers have real appeal, but he's issued 40 walks while striking out 66, and when you translate that to an MLB context, the walk rate blooms to 4.4 per nine while MLB hitters average just 3.2 allowed. His K-BB% translates to 9.4% against a field sitting at 13.5%, and that gap is the whole tension here: the run suppression is holding at AAA but the command profile is the kind that unravels fast when the level gets harder to fool. If the walks tighten, there's a back-of-rotation arm somewhere in this profile; if they don't, the ceiling and floor converge at organizational depth.
